rv.q: The touring cast certainly lives up to all the requirements of the piece, from their macho good looks to their inner sensitivity to the quality of their voices.
Taymor's cast fires on all cylinders.
There are some shows worth seeing and others we simply shouldn't miss. THE OUTSIDERS is the latter.

The acting was smart, classy, and easy to follow. The singing was excellent. And, most importantly, I either completely missed it the first time or simply didn't appreciate it enough—the choreography is outstanding.
As I said, this production of THE OUTSIDERS at Shea's is a benchmark musical we’ll be talking about for years.
Not only is the visual and auditory presentation exquisite, but the story is heartfelt; it's one of loss and prejudice, longing and ambition, violence and poverty, brotherhood and belonging.

The Outsiders is a must-see for anyone who grew up loving the novel or film and it's also a fascinating example of how theatrical technology can evolve while still giving the deep pleasures that only theater brings.

The Outsiders is an authentic American theatrical experience, exposing our societal failures, and holding up the promises of every individual, no matter the side of the tracks where fate led them to be born.
It was one of those moments that reminded me why I love theatre so much.
It's both spectacular and intimate at the same time.
“The Outsiders'” staging turns a little into a lot as the cast deftly moves props around to create a variety of settings, from a park to a drive-in movie theater.

Hinton’s themes around identity, belonging, socioeconomic division, and found family are as resonant now as they were almost 60 years ago. Its teen angst is familiar, maybe too familiar at times, but the production’s staging and performances lend it a physical immediacy that keeps it from feeling stale or cliché.
Decades after Hinton’s novel became required reading and Coppola’s film introduced the Brat Pack, the musical is a reminder of the enduring power of “The Outsiders.

While you can easily draw comparisons to the popular “West Side Story,” with the teenage gangs and the star crossed relationships between the male and female leads, the most memorable parts of the book for me- the insecure contemplation and intimate conversations- were not something I could easily envision translating to a big Broadway musical.

By the end, the set grows more fragmented as the memory fades into the reality of Ponyboy’s present. We watch him read his story-in-progress from his beloved notebook, which turns out to be the first few lines of Hinton’s novel and how the show began a couple hours ago.
By and large, the songs, by Jamestown Revival members Jonathan Clay, Zach Chance and Levine, may not stick with you long after seeing the show, but they serve the story very well.
"The Outsiders" works as well as it does due to the efforts of the creative team in establishing a cruel world where violence often takes the place of open dialogue.
My disappointment in the show has to do with the story, not the cast.

Music and lyrics by Jamestown Revival (Jonathan Clay and Zach Chance) and Justin Levine, book by Adam Rapp and Levine, based on the S.E. Hinton novel and Francis Ford Coppola movie, directed by Danya Taymor.
